INTRODUCTION
Welcome to Hope & Fear

Daggerheart: Hope & Fear is an expansion that provides additional content for players and GMs
who own the Daggerheart Core Set.

A DAGGERHEART EXPANSION
We’re so glad you’re here. This book is an expansion, and
therefore assumes you own the Daggerheart Core Set and
are looking for more content to include in your campaigns.
Since the game launched, our team has been very excited to
continue building for the system, and we hope this expansion
helps enhance your Daggerheart games. As always, the golden
rule applies to all the work we’ve done here: Use what brings
your table joy, and leave behind what doesn’t.
WHAT’S INCLUDED IN THIS
EXPANSION?
Hope & Fear provides the following collection of new material
to supplement the Daggerheart Core Set:
• The Dread domain
• The assassin, brawler, warlock, and witch classes
• Six ancestries and six communities
• A set of transformations available for characters: the
demigod, ghost, reanimated, shapeshifter, vampire, and
werewolf
• A collection of equipment and loot
• Numerous adversaries and environments
• Four campaign frames
HOW SHOULD I IMPLEMENT
THESE ELEMENTS?
All aspects of this book are intended as additional
options for your table to choose from or use when playing
Daggerheart. As always, the GM should decide which
elements fit the style of the campaign they’re running and
offer those options to their players. Just because they’re in
this book doesn’t mean they should automatically be added
to every campaign.
If you’re playing or running Daggerheart for the first time,
we recommend beginning with the core set. The elements
included in this expansion are designed to build on the
choices and complexity of the base game in a way that
might not be as easy to navigate for a first-time GM or
player. For example, including all twenty-four ancestry
options or all thirteen class options at character creation
for a first-time group can feel very overwhelming. Consider
implementing new options from Hope & Fear after you have
at least a few games of Daggerheart under your belt.
4
Introduction

DREAD DOMAIN
Some class options in this book use a domain
called Dread. Dread is the domain of nightmares
and fear. Those who choose this path can call forth
monstrosities, enfeeble their foes, and channel
terrifying magic to destroy their enemies. Dread
grants its adherents power over forces most are
too afraid to employ.
Dread domain cards are included in this expansion,
and the Dread domain features can additionally be
found in the appendix on page 180.

Chapter 1: Character Options

ASSASSIN
Assassins are masters at inflicting deadly injuries with precise
strikes. Unlike those who wield violence as only a means to an
end, assassins approach death as a profession. Many members
of this class believe theirs is a worthy, if not sacred, trade, and
some join guilds to hone their craft, define their beliefs, and earn
money. People from all walks of life hire assassins for their skills:
powerful rulers looking to avoid all-out war, business leaders
seeking to eliminate the competition, and even average people
hoping to settle a grudge. Often, an assassin is the last resort for
killing those previously believed to be unkillable. While some of
these deadly professionals will destroy anyone in their path for
the right reasons or the right price, others hold strict moral codes
or personal rules that dictate their targets. Those who end up the
target of an assassin should count themselves among the dead.
DOMAINS
Blade and Midnight
STARTING EVASION
12
STARTING HIT POINTS
5
CLASS ITEMS
A list of names with several marked off or a rusted blade
inscribed with an insignia
ASSASSIN’S HOPE FEATURE
Deadly Determination: Spend 3 Hope to clear 2 Stress.
CLASS FEATURES
Marked for Death
On a successful weapon attack, you can mark a Stress to
make the target Marked for Death. When you deal damage to a
target you’ve Marked for Death, add a number of d4s equal to
your tier to the damage roll.
You can have only one adversary Marked for Death at a
time. This condition lasts until you take a rest, the current
adversary Marked for Death is defeated, or the GM spends a
number of Fear equal to your tier to clear it.
Get In & Get Out
Spend a Hope to ask the GM for a quick or inconspicuous way
into or out of a place you can see. The next roll you make that
acts on this information has advantage.

Chapter 1: Classes

ASSASSIN SUBCLASSES
Choose either the Executioners Guild or
Poisoners Guild subclass.
EXECUTIONERS GUILD
Play the Executioners Guild if you want to strike down your
targets with lethal precision.
SPELLCAST TRAIT
Agility
FOUNDATION FEATURES
First Strike: The first time in a scene you succeed on an attack,
you deal double damage.
Ambush: Your “Marked for Death” feature uses d6s instead of
d4s.
SPECIALIZATION FEATURES
Death Strike: When you deal Severe damage to a creature,
you can mark a Stress to force them to mark an additional Hit
Point.
Scorpion’s Poise: You gain a +2 bonus to your Evasion against
attacks made by a creature you’ve Marked for Death.
MASTERY FEATURES
True Strike: Once per long rest when you fail an attack, you
can spend a Hope to make it a success instead.
Backstab: Your “Marked for Death” feature uses d8s instead
of d6s.

POISONERS GUILD
Play the Poisoners Guild if you want to debilitate your targets
with punishing afflictions.
SPELLCAST TRAIT
Knowledge
FOUNDATION FEATURE
Toxic Concoctions: Mark a Stress to place 1d4+1 tokens on
this card. When you make a successful weapon attack, you
can spend a token to afflict the target with a poison. You know
these poisons:
•	 Ghost Petal: The target becomes temporarily Vulnerable.
•	 Grave Spore: The target must also mark a Stress.
•	 Leech Weed: You deal an extra 1d6 damage on this attack.
When you take a long rest, clear all unspent tokens.
SPECIALIZATION FEATURES
Poison Compendium: You also know these poisons:
•	 Midnight Vine: The target has disadvantage on attack rolls
until it marks a Stress to clear this condition.
•	 Gorgon Root: The target becomes temporarily Restrained.
Twin Fang: When you afflict a target Marked for Death with a
poison you know, you can spend an additional token to also
inflict the effect of a second poison you know.
MASTERY FEATURES
Venomancer: You also know these poisons:
•	 Blight Seed: The target gains a −3 penalty to their damage
thresholds until the end of the scene. This effect can’t
stack.
•	 Fear Leaf: You deal extra damage equal to the result of
your Fear Die on this attack.
•	 Corpse Thorn: The target gains disadvantage on reaction
rolls until the end of the scene.
Adder’s Blessing: You are immune to poisons and other toxins.

BACKGROUND QUESTIONS
Answer any of the following background questions. You can
also create your own questions.
•	 You once killed someone you were close to. What
happened, and how did it change you?
•	 What organization trained you in the art of killing, and
how did you become a member?
•	 Throughout your career, one target has eluded you.
Who are they, and how have they slipped through
your fingers?
CONNECTIONS
Ask your fellow players one of the following questions for
their character to answer, or create your own questions.
•	 I’ve killed someone for you. Who were they?
•	 How did you save me when I was on the brink of
death? What have I promised you as repayment?
•	 What secret about myself did I tell you, and how did it
change your view of me?

Chapter 1: Classes

BRAWLER
Experts in unarmed combat, brawlers hone their bodies into
lethal weapons. Whether they learned from formal training,
studied with a mentor, or picked up their skills one fight at a
time, the process is always rigorous as brawlers develop their
body and mind to work as one. Brawlers are valued for their
power and versatility and typically join a party or a cause when
the need or desire arises. Because a brawler’s body is their
strongest weapon, they typically seek out new challenges or
consistent sparring partners so they can maintain their skills
and add new techniques to their repertoire. Though they might
appear unassuming to those accustomed to foes who are armed
to the teeth, brawlers often accomplish more with bare knuckles
than an average soldier with a sword.
DOMAINS
Valor and Bone
STARTING EVASION
10
STARTING HIT POINTS
6
CLASS ITEMS
Hand wraps from a mentor or a book about your secret hobby
BRAWLER’S HOPE FEATURE
Square Up: Spend 3 Hope to intimidate a target within Close
range, making them temporarily Vulnerable.
CLASS FEATURES
I Am the Weapon
Your barehanded attacks are as strong as any blade. You have
a primary weapon called Brawler’s Strike equipped while you
have no other Active Weapons. It uses a trait of your choice,
has Melee range, and deals d8+d6 physical damage using your
Proficiency (both the d8 and d6 scale off your Proficiency).
While this weapon is active, you gain a +1 bonus to your
Evasion.
Combo Strike
After rolling damage on a successful attack with a Melee
weapon, you can mark a Stress to start a combo strike. When
you do, roll your Combo Die and note the result, then continue
rolling your Combo Die until the result of your latest roll is
lower than the roll that preceded it. You deal extra damage
equal to the total of all rolled Combo Die results on this
attack. The results can’t be modified by any means.
Your Combo Die starts as a d4. Once per tier, you can
increase your Combo Die by one step as a level
advancement option.

Chapter 1: Classes

BRAWLER SUBCLASSES
Choose either the Juggernaut or Martial Artist
subclass.
JUGGERNAUT
Play the Juggernaut if you want to pulverize your opponents with
crushing blows.
FOUNDATION FEATURES
Rugged: Gain a permanent +3 bonus to your Severe damage
threshold.
Overwhelm: When you succeed on an attack against a target,
you can spend a Hope to throw the target within Close range
or to force them to mark a Stress.
SPECIALIZATION FEATURES
Surrounded: When you make an attack with a Melee weapon,
you can spend any number of Hope to target an equal number
of additional creatures within Melee range.
Eye for an Eye: Once per rest when an adversary within Melee
range forces you to mark any number of Hit Points, you can
mark a Stress to force them to mark the same number of Hit
Points.
MASTERY FEATURES
Pummeljoy: When you critically succeed on a Melee weapon
attack, you gain an additional Hope, clear an additional Stress,
and gain a +1 bonus to your Proficiency for that attack.
Not Done Yet: When you take Severe damage, you can gain a
Hope or clear a Stress.

MARTIAL ARTIST
Play the Martial Artist if you want to use a variety of fighting
styles to eliminate your foes.
FOUNDATION FEATURE
Stance Fighter: You can channel your inner resolve to shift into
martial stances that grant you special benefits in combat.
Take the Martial Stances sheet and choose two martial
stances from Tier 1. Each time you level up your character,
choose an additional stance from your tier or lower.
SPECIALIZATION FEATURES
Keen Defenses: When you’re targeted by an attack, you can
spend a Focus to gain a bonus to your Evasion equal to your
tier against the attack.
Focus Cannon: Spend a Focus to make an Instinct Roll against
an adversary within Far range. On a success, deal d20+3
magic damage using your Proficiency.
MASTERY FEATURES
Limit Breaker: Once per rest, you can perform an unbelievable
feat of athletic prowess, such as running across water,
leaping between distant rooftops, or scaling a building without
needing to roll. When you do, gain a Hope and clear a Stress.
Flow State: You can mark a Stress instead of spending a
Focus to shift into a different stance. Additionally, you can
spend a Focus instead of marking a Stress to start a combo
strike.

BACKGROUND QUESTIONS
Answer any of the following background questions. You can
also create your own questions.
•	 Where did you spend time during your formative years
that taught you, directly or indirectly, how to fight in
the style you use?
•	 What organization has vowed to kill you on sight, and
what did you do to invoke their ire?
•	 Who did you recently lose a fight to that you’re
desperate for a rematch against?
CONNECTIONS
Ask your fellow players one of the following questions for
their character to answer, or create your own questions.
•	 What is one thing we’re both afraid of?
•	 What do I rely on you for during our travels? How do
you feel about it?
•	 I still haven’t forgiven you for something you said to
me. What was it, and why did you say it?

Chapter 1: Classes

MARTIAL STANCES
When you choose the Martial Artist subclass, take the Martial
Stances sheet to track which stances your character knows.
You can also track which stance you have active and your
current Focus.
STANCES
Stances are special body positionings that enable Martial
Artists to attack, react, or defend in combat. Each stance
grants your character a different ability, bonus, or feature
while active.
You choose two stances from Tier 1 when you first take the
Martial Artist’s subclass foundation card. Mark the circle next
to each to indicate that your character knows and has access
to them. Mark a new stance from your tier or below each time
you gain a level.
FOCUS
Focus represents your character’s poise, clarity, and control.
Once per rest during a moment of calm, you can clear your
mind and refocus your martial instincts. Clear your Focus
track, then roll a number of d6s equal to your Instinct and
gain Focus equal to the highest result rolled. You can hold a
maximum of 6 Focus.
SHIFTING INTO STANCES
You can spend a Focus to shift into a martial stance and gain
its effects. You can shift only into stances you’ve marked as
known. When you shift into a stance, it’s considered your
active stance until you drop out of it.
You can’t shift into or have more than one active stance at a
time. Until you shift into a stance, you are not considered to
be in a stance or to have an active stance.
DROPPING OUT OF STANCES
If you are already in a stance when you shift into a different
stance, you automatically drop out of the previously active
stance. You also drop out of your active stance when you take
Severe damage or mark your last Hit Point. Otherwise, you
drop out of your active stance at the end of the scene. When
you drop out of a stance, you lose any ongoing benefits it
provides.

STANCE FEATURES
The following section lists all martial stances by tier.
TIER 1
Favored: Gain a bonus to damage rolls equal to a trait of your
choice.
Invigorating: On a successful attack, roll a d4. On a result of 4,
gain a Focus.
Quick: When you make an attack, you can spend a Focus or

Reliable: Gain a +1 bonus to your attack rolls.
TIER 2
Aggressive: Gain a −1 penalty to your Evasion. On a successful
attack, roll an additional damage die and discard the lowest
result.
Anchored: Gain a +2 bonus to your damage thresholds. While
in this stance, you can’t be moved against your will.
Defensive: Attack rolls targeting you from within Melee range
have disadvantage unless the attacker marks a Stress to
negate the disadvantage.
Otherworldly: On a successful attack, you can deal physical or
magic damage.
TIER 3
Grappling: On a successful attack within Melee range, you can
spend a Focus or mark a Stress to temporarily Restrain the
target or throw the target up to Close range.
Scary: On a successful attack, the target must mark a Stress.
Stable: You can spend a Focus instead of an Armor Slot to
reduce damage.
Vigilant: When you are targeted by an attack, you can mark a
Stress to gain a d6 bonus to your Evasion against the attack.
TIER 4
Crushing: When you deal Severe damage, you can spend a
Hope to force the target to mark an additional Hit Point.
Exacting: When you roll a 1 on a damage die, you can treat it
as the highest value on the die instead.
Honed: Spend a Focus before you make an attack roll to gain a
+1 bonus to your Proficiency for that attack.
Isolating: Gain advantage on attack rolls when there are no
other creatures within Very Close range of you or your target.

Chapter 1: Classes

WARLOCK
Those who’ve traded their lives—or perhaps even their souls—
to an otherworldly patron in exchange for incredible power are
known as warlocks. Often, these mortals have reached a point
of desperation that leads them to make this sacrifice: they hope
to protect themselves or a loved one, aid their community, seek
vengeance, increase their status, or otherwise further their
ambitions. The powerful entities they entreat are as varied as
the warlocks themselves: gods, spirits, demons, or other beings
unknown to even the mortal who makes the pact. The entities
each have their own sphere of influence that defines their
otherworldly power, and those that collect souls are rarely known
for their benevolence. Thus, a warlock’s power is defined by the
relationship they maintain with their benefactor. Despite their
terrifying magic, warlocks might find that someone or something
else is pulling their strings.
DOMAINS
Dread and Grace
STARTING EVASION
11
STARTING HIT POINTS
5
CLASS ITEMS
A carving that symbolizes your patron or a ring you can’t
remove
WARLOCK’S HOPE FEATURE
Patron’s Boon: When you fail a roll, you can spend 3 Hope to
reroll with advantage.
CLASS FEATURES
Patron’s Pact
You have committed yourself to a supernatural entity­—such
as a god, fae, or demon—in exchange for power. Write their
name on your character sheet, then work with your GM to
determine their sphere of influence (such as Nature, Chaos,

WITCH
Witches are magical practitioners who commune with the
forces of nature and entities from realms beyond. These
spellcasters call forth power through craft, combining
the tangible and ephemeral by casting spells, murmuring
incantations, creating talismans, weaving illusions, and
maintaining other personalized practices. They can protect
their allies and harm their enemies by invoking powerful
forces beyond themselves—supernatural beings such as
ancestors, deities, or aspects of nature. Often, their magical
knowledge is passed down from these entities or through

groups known as covens. Witches are frequently feared and
misunderstood, as their methods can appear mysterious,
strange, and even macabre to the uninitiated. Whichever path

AETHERIS
Aetheris are humanoids most easily recognized by their wings
and sacred markings. They are the descendants of angels from
the Hallows Above. Aetheris are typically 5 to 7 feet tall, and
some may have elongated limbs. They often have vibrantly
colored eyes, hair, and skin, though their coloring can include
earth tones and pastels. Many members of this ancestry are
born with sacred markings—such as glowing sigils or intricate
patterns of lines and symbols—but all aetheris develop them
as they mature. These symbols change as they age, often
because of prophecies, revelations, and divine guidance from
the Hallows Above.
All aetheris have a “hallowed aura” that can manifest
voluntarily, such as when they invoke their power, or
involuntarily, such as when they feel elation or other strong
emotions. When they call forth this radiance, their eyes
and bodies might glow, their markings might become more
prominent or shift across their skin, or they might have a halo
appear atop or around their head. These halos are as unique
as a fingerprint and may share similarities with other family
members. Perhaps due to their angelic lineage, aetheris
usually live for 350 years, and they retain a youthful glow even
as they age.
Angels in the Hallows Above
When the New Gods won the Divine War, many Faint
Divinities who fought alongside them also came to reside
in the Hallows Above. These Faint Divinities are known as
“angels” in part because many of them act as messengers
to the Mortal Realm on behalf of the New Gods. Stories
say angels can pass between the Hallows Above and the
Mortal Realm without the need for a personal sacrifice.
Others claim that the New Gods merely use the Faint
Divinities to make the journeys on their behalf, expending
the essence of their lessers in order to avoid paying
the cost themselves. For more on the cosmology of
Daggerheart, see page 11 of the core rulebook.
Their wings come in a variety of shapes and sizes, with
the most common being feathered.

ELEMENTAL KIN
Elemental kin are humanoid mortals descended from powerful
supernatural entities known as elementals—embodiments
of the fundamental forces that shape the Mortal Realm (such
as earth, air, fire, and water). These “kin” manifest forces
differently, with some appearing more or less humanoid than
others, but they all have a lineage that grants them unique
ways to harness and influence their elemental heritage.
At birth, elemental kin closely resemble the element they
embody, then become increasingly humanoid as they mature
through early childhood. As they grow, their appearance
manifests unique characteristics that identify them as
elemental kin, such as crystal formations across a stonekin’s
shoulders or a skykin’s ever-present breeze tousling their
hair. While adult elemental kin are predominantly flesh and
blood, small portions of their bodies momentarily shift into an
elemental state in times of great emotion. Elemental kin with
limb differences, or who lost a limb at some point in their life,
can also manipulate a small amount of their element to help
them accomplish a variety of tasks.
Some elemental kins’ physical characteristics are passed
down through families, such as one family of earthkin bearing
shifting skin with the texture of sand, while another bears
marble patterns. Additionally, families often develop their
own unique communication styles that use their elemental
influence. For example, emberkin might express excitement
with flares of fire from their eyes, while tidekin might use
currents of color over their bodies to communicate subtle
messages.
Though their lifespans vary, all elemental kin return to their
element upon their death.

EARTHKIN
Earthkin are humanoids whose bodies are made of flesh and earth.
Descended from earth elementals, members of this ancestry are
formed of flesh and rock, crystal, clay, soil, sand, or a mixture
of these materials. Some are primarily flesh and blood with just
one earthen feature, such as skin the color or texture of stone or
crystal formations that adorn their heads like hair. Others are a
combination, often asymmetrical unions of muscle and natural
minerals. Still others are almost entirely soil and stone. Earthkin
might choose to mold and decorate the mineral portions of their
form by carving designs, embedding gems or metals, or even
planting seeds that bloom into adorning foliage. Their coloring
comes from their elemental lineage, as even those who are more
flesh than earth come in hues reminiscent of marble, gemstones,
sand, soil, and more.
These kin begin their lives as small lumps of earth, such as a
boulder, a ball of clay, or a crystal cluster. Though they’ll develop
their more humanoid features fairly quickly, earthkin age slowly for
most of their approximately 300-year lifespan. Their average height
at adulthood ranges from 5 to 61⁄2 feet tall, and the shape of their
body is strongly influenced by the primary material it’s composed of.
Many earthkin’s injuries appear like fissures in stone; even long after
the initial damage has healed, these cracks continue to slowly repair.
When they die, earthkin eventually crumble into piles of earth.

Emberkin are humanoids whose bodies are made of flesh and

Being part of a duneborne community means you’ve made

FREEBORNE
Being part of a freeborne community means you’re
from a collective that once lived under tyrannical
rule but is now liberated. Though no two freeborne
enclaves are the same, all are unified by the
experience of fighting to preserve their culture
while others tried to eradicate it. Whether due
to their religion, resources, location, or culture,
freeborne groups were once subjugated by another
community. For some, this subjugation might
have only recently ended; for others, even if their
freedom has been long-won, the scars of tyranny
can last, bonding together families and neighbors
for decades or even generations. Many freeborne
collectives unify in and rebuild the lands reclaimed
from their oppressors or in a homeland they were
taken from. Others see “home” as a collection of
people who care for one another, no matter where
they reside.
Many freeborne passionately celebrate their
unique holidays, art, food, decor, and other
customs, whether they’re enjoying long-held
traditions or new practices born from liberation.
Their past experiences often forge in them a fierce
protectiveness of their community and an equally
strong fervor to celebrate their culture.
Freeborne are often optimistic, guarded, courageous,
joyful, subversive, and traumatized.

FROSTBORNE

Being part of a frostborne community means you come from a place of snow and ice. Forged in bitter and unrelenting cold,
frostborne communities are accustomed to surviving in the harshest conditions. The glaciers and tundras they call home usually
lack wood, so these collectives use more readily available materials such as ice, stone, bone, and animal pelts to make shelter
and conserve heat. They are adept at ensuring their supplies go a long way and that all their people have access to the essentials
needed to survive. As part of their systems of survival, many frostborne closely track weather patterns, the rising and setting

HEARTHBORNE
Being part of a hearthborne community means you come from humble origins, having lived
in a modest village or quaint countryside. These communities are often small groups that
live in resource-rich, peaceful areas that allow families and neighbors the time to develop
close-knit relationships rather than compete over scarce supplies. Hearthborne communities
are largely agrarian and pastoral, focusing the layout of their villages around their plants and
animals. The town centers typically feature a collection of locally owned shops with skilled
artisans such as blacksmiths, cobblers, alchemists, and the like. Sometimes, hearthborne
communities have distant but powerful rulers who own the land the villagers work and
live on—in those cases, resources are controlled by the wealthy even though the labor is
performed by locals, and workers might struggle to afford the basics they need to survive.
While some hearthborne individuals can be mistrustful of outsiders, most are known for
being welcoming, peaceful, and hospitable.
Hearthborne are often careful, generous, insular, loquacious, smiley, and traditional.

REBORNE
You were once a member of a different community that you’re
no longer part of. Unlike members of collectives who are allied
by familiarity, shared location, history, and culture, reborne
are individuals who might never meet and are unified only
by their shared experience of solitude. Whether they left by
choice or were ripped from their community, all reborne are
disconnected from the place where they once belonged, and
they carry that wound with them.
Some reborne are isolated from their community because they
chose to reject or renounce it, or they could have been forcibly
expelled by other members. These instances are often due to
a conflict, such as clashing ideological differences, a falling out
with their people, or an incident that forced them to depart.
Other reborne have no knowledge of their culture, either
due to their upbringing or perhaps because they lost their
memory through injury or magic. Some have even returned
from beyond the veil after death with no recollection of their
previous life—or the culture that shaped it.
Often, reborne individuals tirelessly search for their past
or feel that they’ll never belong in a collective, but all are
afforded the opportunity to turn toward the future and
redefine themselves while building new bonds with those they
come to know and love.
Reborne are often curious, hopeful, innocent, isolated, mournful,
and uncanny.

When to Choose the Reborne Community
Some players might want to choose the reborne community
because they’re developing a character who was expelled
from or willingly left their home. While this choice is
supported by both the mechanics and the narrative of the
card, it’s not the only way to craft that character arc in
Daggerheart.
Many people leave their communities of origin or allegiance,
either due to a difference in beliefs or a move to a new
location. Even a disagreement with loved ones can lead
people to turn the page on a new chapter in their lives.
When someone leaves the culture they were raised in, that
culture stays with them throughout their life, influencing
their approach to the world. If you want to build a character
who’s estranged from their home, you might be better
served by taking the community card for the collective your
PC left behind and conveying the friction they feel between
their old culture and their new way of life.
If you take this approach, you can replace your current
community card with the reborne card at a pivotal moment
of growth to signify your PC’s separation from their former
life and their new approach to the world. If this character
arc appeals to you, talk to your GM to see how you can work
it into your campaign, both mechanically and narratively.

WARBORNE
Being part of a warborne community means you come from a place that
is, or was, ravaged by war. These groups might be composed of civilians
who live in an active warzone, soldiers who served together in the armed
forces, or citizens of nations that have been in conflict for decades.
Whether civilian or military, warborne are typically skilled in self-defense,
even if their tactics are focused on avoidance rather than offensive action.
Warborne defending their homeland are known for using their
environment to their advantage, while invading warborne might rely
entirely on their military might. No matter their origin, the life of a
warborne is defined at least in part by resourcefulness. Those who live
in an occupied territory might need to undertake massive reconstruction
efforts to repair and preserve homes, farms, workplaces, or cultural
monuments—the remnants of one building often become the materials
to repair another. Meanwhile, warborne who are part of an invading army
typically carry few personal possessions and must rely on scavenging the
warzones they occupy. Whether they find themselves on the winning or
losing side of a conflict, those from warborne communities are likely to
bear trauma for the rest of their lives, their sense of safety and mortality
forever marred by the mass casualties and destruction of war.
Warborne are often strategic, devastated, determined, calculating,
unwavering, and devoted.

TRANSFORMATIONs

Transformations represent specific changes or augmentations of a Daggerheart character, often
through magical means.

Transformations represent a fundamental shift in your
character and how they interact with the world. These are
optional aspects of a character’s identity that the GM can
give out during a campaign as part of the narrative or, at their
discretion, present as an option during character creation.
Transformations provide both a mechanical benefit and a
drawback. Taking a transformation card requires you to buy
into the concept of the exchange, taking on the burden to
reap the benefit. Because of this, we recommend you remind
your GM of your transformation’s negative effects whenever
they’re relevant to help both you and the GM fulfill the fiction
of the transformation.
Like ancestry and community cards, a transformation card
doesn’t count against your domain card limit. When your
character gains a transformation, add the card to your loadout
as if it were part of your character’s heritage. Consider how
this transformation changes your character physically and
psychologically—if you need inspiration, each transformation
includes questions to help you.
While some transformations offer expanded power or
unique narrative implications, unless stated otherwise in
their features, no transformation prohibits a PC from being
affected by damage or keeps them from making death moves.
If there are details you’d like to incorporate into your character
that go beyond the features on a transformation card, work
with your GM to explore how they might manifest in your
campaign’s narrative.
A PC can have only one transformation.

GRANTING TRANSFORMATIONS
GMs should discuss transformations with your players before
incorporating them into your campaign. Transformations
deeply impact a PC’s narrative journey, so it’s best to ensure
this aspect of the game supports the story your players want
to tell and is something they’ll enjoy.
Some of the transformations presented here are easy to
introduce during a campaign as a narrative development.
For example, the vampire or werewolf transformation could
be gained when the campaign’s major villain targets a PC
with a significant attack. A PC who gains the reanimated
or ghost transformation might have died in a place of great
magic or made a story-altering bargain in exchange for their
resurrection. These transformations can also be part of
character creation. Maybe a PC was born a werewolf and
seeks to control this aspect of their lineage, or a PC is a long-
dead ghost who haunts the party to protect the living.
Some transformations are more likely to be taken at character
creation, such as the shapeshifter or demigod. However, they
can still be introduced as a character twist during a campaign.
It’s ultimately up to you which transformations are available at
character creation and how they become available throughout
play—decide what works best for you, your players, and the
story you’re telling together.

DEMIGOD
Demigods are mortal creatures whose veins flow with the
blood of the gods. They typically gain their power from divine
parentage, accomplishing an incredible feat, or receiving a gift
from a god. Many demigods appear as a typical member of
their mortal ancestry, but all possess a subtle luminosity and
a gleam in their eyes. They’re also known to have pearlescent
or metallic skin, and they might grow in size or gain physical
features related to their power when it reveals itself. Because
they share the blood of a Faint Divinity, a Forgotten God, a
New God, or any other deity, no two demigods look the same.
Demigods are bestowed with a fragment of deific power, but
not everything a demigod inherits is a blessing. Though they
often excel at tasks they’re well suited for, the expectations
set upon them are often difficult and costly to live up to.
Examining Divinity in Daggerheart
In Daggerheart, PCs gain divine power in a number of
ways. It can come through their ancestry, such as aetheris
or infernis, who are distant descendants of the Faint
Divinities. It can come through a character’s community,
such as an orderborne religious collective whose faith
inspires them. It can come through a character’s class,
such as the seraph or warlock, who dedicate themselves
to an otherworldly entity. It could also come through a
transformation, such as demigod, which imposes a heavy
burden to counterbalance the divine blessings.
For example, a player could build an Orderborne Aetheris
Demigod Pact of the Wrathful Warlock, where each
aspect of their character relates to a different source of
divinity.

GHOST
Ghosts are the spirits of the once-living who are bound to
the Mortal Realm. They could be called forth after passing
through the veil of death with necromantic rites, alchemical
experimentation, the desperation of a loved one—or they
may never have passed through the veil at all. Those who met
a horrific end, were killed with a cursed weapon, or died in
a place of power might have become trapped in the Mortal
Realm instead of passing on.
Because they occupy the space between life and death, a ghost
can shift between the physical and the spectral and, at times,
pass through solid objects. While some ghosts are almost
indistinguishable from the living, others emanate spectral
auras, appear desaturated in color, or bear physical evidence
of their cause of death. When a ghost becomes incorporeal—
which can occur at will, due to heightened emotions, or
seemingly at random—they might appear semitranslucent,
like a breath of fog that could dissipate in the wind.
Some ghosts return for revenge, some to save a loved one,
and others to meet a goal or discover hidden knowledge. Their
drive to accomplish this goal is the force that allows them to
exist in the Mortal Realm. When they complete that goal, their
work is done, and they immediately pass beyond the veil of
death.
TRANSFORMATION FEATURES
Unfinished Business: Work with your GM to decide what
purpose or desire keeps you bound to the Mortal Realm. When
you fulfill it, you cross through the veil of death.
Ephemeral: Your body wavers in and out of being corporeal.
You are resistant to physical damage, take double magic
damage, and can mark 2 Stress to momentarily pass through
a solid object.

REANIMATED
Reanimated are corpses who have been brought back to life.
Whether through a spell, a holy ritual, arcane experimentation,
or other unnatural methods, these mortals have returned
from beyond the veil of death as undead and are bound to
their decaying bodies. Newly reanimated are more likely to
look like a typical member of their ancestry, but as they go on,
they must patch and repair their bodies with bones, flesh, and
other materials harvested from the recently deceased. While
some repair their wounds and decay with needle, thread, and
herbs, others use magic to incorporate these materials into
themselves.
Many stories of the reanimated describe them as possessing
increased durability or, in some cases, immunity to pain.
This may be true for some reanimated, but many experience
prolonged agony—whether from the physical echoes of their
own demise, the discomfort of moving a decomposing body,
the trouble controlling their amalgamated parts, or the mental
anguish of being forcibly pulled back from death into a second
life.

SHAPESHIFTER
Shapeshifters are creatures who can change their physical
form. Whether they were born with this ability, gained it as
a result of magical craft or a curse, or received this power
from an otherworldly entity, shapeshifters have a unique
relationship with their identity. Because shapeshifters can
transform into any ancestry—one moment living as a small
and nimble faerie and the next as a large and tough galapa—
their experiences with the outside world can vary greatly from
day to day.
While a shapeshifter is typically indistinguishable from another
member of the ancestry they transform into, each shapeshifter
has one characteristic that doesn’t change no matter their
form, such as their eyes, their coloring, or a unique birthmark.
They also can’t mimic a specific person’s appearance, as they
become a different version of themselves in a new body.
Taking on a new form also doesn’t allow them to immediately
have or use all the new form’s characteristics—they must
focus their efforts on the physical characteristics they most
want to use. Shapeshifters might need time to learn how
to embody a new form, sometimes leading to an uncanny
appearance or behavior until they’re accustomed to their body.

cloud of magic while another
reassembles themself.

VAMPIRE
Vampires are undead creatures with sharp fangs who feed on
the blood of the living. They aren’t born, but created—sired
by another vampire through a bite and exchange of blood,
transformed through an occult ritual, or changed through
other mysterious methods. Because those who become
vampires die and come back as supernatural entities, they
must consume the blood—the life essence—of others to
survive.
At first glance, many vampires are indistinguishable from
typical members of their ancestry. Beyond their telltale fangs,
they can be affected by their vampirism in myriad subtle or
conspicuous ways, displaying traits such as sallow skin, visible
veins, eyes that shine in the dark, or, in some cases, enhanced
beauty. Depending on the nature of their vampiric origin,
individuals may stop aging at the time of their transformation
and remain vibrant and powerful long after their cohorts
have succumbed to the ravages of time. No matter their
appearance, all vampires possess enhanced abilities that can
result in a terrifying end for their targets.

WEREWOLF
Werewolves are creatures who transform into large
supernatural wolves. While some are born werewolves, others
undergo this transformation because of a curse, an infection
through another werewolf’s bite, or another unnatural cause.
Werewolves look like typical members of their ancestry
until they shift, whereupon they transform into a massive
otherworldly wolf. Some might even take on a shape that is an
amalgamation of their ancestry and their wolf form. Stories
describe werewolves shifting with the phases of the moon,
though an individual’s experience with this change varies based
on the cause of their transformation.
Werewolves often struggle to control their hunting instinct and
violence while in their wolf form, and they must have immense
self-discipline, use significant energy, or resort to fleeing or
locking themselves away to avoid harming their loved ones.
The longer a werewolf has experience with their condition, the
more likely they are to have developed methods of controlling
themselves.

CHAPTER THREE:
Adversaries & Environments

This chapter presents the stat blocks for new adversaries and environments.

New Adversary Features
The following section details the new adversary features used in this expansion.
POOL
A pool is a collection of tokens shared by multiple adversaries.
Each pool has a unique name, which is typically the name
shared by the adversaries it affects. Unlike standard adversary
tokens, pool tokens are not placed on a stat block; instead,
the GM collects them in a separate location. Pools are empty
when the scene begins and cleared when the scene ends.
Adversary Stat Blocks

EVOLUTION
Evolutions are features that alter an adversary when certain
trigger conditions are met. When triggered, an evolution
feature usually clears HP or Stress, alters the stats of the
adversary’s standard attack, and gives the adversary access to
new features. An adversary’s evolution can’t be triggered more
than once in a scene.

journey.

How does it feel being in someone else’s skin? If you could choose to

events and figures in the Moon Kingdom’s history and gains
1d4 Hope, which they can distribute among PCs they share
their visions with.
• Success with Hope: The PC receives clear information about
key events and figures in the Moon Kingdom’s history.
• Any roll with Fear: The PC receives brief flashes and
sensations related to the kingdom’s cataclysmic end. If the
roll was a failure, the PC takes 4d10+5 magic damage as the
visions assault their psyche.
What does this machinery look like, and how does it work? What do
the PCs learn about the Moon Kingdom’s history?
The Moon Queen’s Tomb - Reaction: The Moon Kingdom’s final
ruler has been preserved in a selenite coffin deep within the
citadel. On a roll with Fear to investigate her chamber, her
baleful shade awakens and attacks the party. Summon the
Moon Queen’s Spirit (Arch-Necromancer) next to her coffin and
immediately spotlight her.
Who buried her here, and why? Can she be resurrected, or is
destroying her spirit the only path forward?

111
Chapter 3: Tier 4 Environments

REALM OF THE DEAD
Tier 4 Traversal
A seemingly infinite expanse of still water without color or laughter.
Impulses: Drown in despair, leech life, tempt into endless slumber
Difficulty: 20
Potential Adversaries: Any (see “Death-Touched Denizens”)
FEATURES
Sea of Gloom - Passive: This realm is a boundless silver ocean
blanketed in a gray gloom with no visible stars or horizon. The
subtle current pulls inexorably at the PCs’ legs, but it’s too gentle
to disturb the flat, mirrored surface of the water. Action rolls to
navigate this realm have disadvantage.
What dangers lie below the surface? How does one find the edge of a
world without end, and what lies beyond it?
The Burden of Wakefulness - Passive: It’s impossible to sleep here.
When the party rests, each PC can choose only one downtime
move.
What thoughts keep the PCs awake here? How can they support one
another without succumbing to hopelessness themselves?
Death-Touched Denizens - Passive: All mortal creatures eventually
pass through this place on their journey to the other side, but
those who linger or wander become warped and mutated by the
gloom. Any adversaries the party encounters here are Faded.
Describe how their time here has warped them into something
worse than dead. When a PC takes damage from a Faded
adversary’s attack, they must also mark a Stress. If a PC is
defeated here, they become a Faded adversary controlled by the
GM instead of making a death move.
Why do these creatures refuse to move on? Is there any pattern to the
forms the gloom fades them into?
The Chill of Death - Action: Spend a Fear to force a PC to make a
Presence Reaction Roll as the Sea of Gloom leeches the warmth
from their blood and bones. On a failure, they take 4d10 direct
magic damage. On a success, they must mark a Stress.
What does it feel like to have the will to live forcibly drained from
you? How do you focus through the despair?
Abandon All Hope - Reaction: When a PC spends Hope in the
Realm of the Dead, they must roll a d6. On an odd result, they
must spend an additional Hope or lose the benefit of the Hope
they already spent.
What regrets gnaw at the edge of your consciousness while you’re
here? What memories still tether you to the Mortal Realm?

REALM OF THE DEAD

Chapter 3: Tier 4 Environments

TIME COURT
Tier 4 Event
One or more PCs are forcibly plucked from the timeline and put on
trial for crimes against continuity.
Impulses: Find the truth, mete out justice, nullify their powers
Difficulty: 20
Potential Adversaries: Judge (Monarch), Jury (Hallowed Choir),
Executioners (Temporal Enforcers)
FEATURES
Out of Time - Passive: The trial takes place in a pocket dimension
that exists beyond the influence of the other realms. While here,
PCs can’t use their features and abilities. Each player must put
their Domain cards in their vault.
What besides the courtroom resides in this pocket dimension? What
powers maintain the universal barrier protecting this place?
Trial by Jury - Passive: At the end of the proceedings, a jury votes
whether to acquit or convict the party. When the court is called
to order, have the prosecution present its case against the PCs
and start a Countdown (9). It ticks down when a PC makes an
action roll. When it triggers, the PCs and GM roll their Judgment
Dice. If the party’s total result meets or exceeds the GM’s, the
jury acquits them.
Which PCs are put on trial? What are they accused of? What
potential penalties would a guilty verdict bring?
Counsel for the Defense - Passive: A PC can make an action
roll to argue for their innocence (such as a Knowledge Roll
to interpret the letter of the law, a Presence Roll to play on
the jury’s emotions, or an Instinct Roll to point out holes in
the prosecution’s case). On a success, the party gains a d6
Judgment Die. On a critical success, they gain two. On a failure,
the prosecution rebuts the PC’s argument, and you gain a d6
Judgment Die.
What is the weakest part of the prosecution’s case? What is the
strongest part of the party’s defense?
Counsel for the Prosecution - Action: The prosecution introduces
a damning piece of evidence (such as an eyewitness testimony,
test results, or a physical exhibit taken from the scene of the
crime), and you gain a d6 Judgment Die. A PC can mark a Stress
to attempt a rebuttal of the evidence with a Knowledge, Instinct,
or Presence Reaction Roll. On a success, the party gains the
Judgment Die instead of you. On a failure, you gain an additional
d6 Judgment Die.
Who leads the prosecution, and what is their relationship to the Time
Council? What magic or technology does this court rely on to present
and record evidence?
“Order in the Court!” - Reaction: When the PCs attempt to escape
or end the trial through force, summon a number of Temporal
Enforcers equal to the number of PCs in the scene within Close
range and immediately spotlight one.
Is this court’s authority worthy of respect? What besides the might
of the Time Council and its enforcers justifies their control over the
timeline?

CHAPTER FOUR:
CAMPAIGN FRAMES

When starting a Daggerheart campaign, you might wish to begin with a campaign frame.
Four campaign frames are presented here in order of complexity.

CASTLE HIGH
In a modern fantasy world, teenagers attend a boarding school
in the clouds—sneaking out of class to fly brooms, explore
floating islands, and save their friends.
Designed by Rowan Hall, Mikey Hamm, Cass Rea, and Spenser Starke
Complexity Rating: •
The Pitch:
In a modern world of knights and cars, wands and flip phones,
there’s no better place to study magic than the floating school
known as Castle High. Drifting among the mysterious ruins of
the ancient world and modern settlements that populate the
clouds, this school and its surroundings hold secrets, danger,
and something more sinister. A string of disappearances has
recently plagued the school, and no one knows who or what is
behind it—or who will disappear next.
In a Castle High campaign, you’ll play adventurous high
schoolers who take magic classes, explore sky islands, and
search for their missing classmates.
This campaign frame starts on page 116.
REIGN OF THE WEREDRAGON
In a land ruled by a violent weredragon tyrant, heroes ordained
by the stars to defeat her must rise to the challenge and defend
their people.
Designed by Jeremy Crawford, Rowan Hall, Christopher Perkins, and
Spenser Starke
Complexity Rating: ••
The Pitch:
Once upon a time, in the peaceful land of Whelvia, a powerful
sorceress named Forlorne Lykona deceived the country’s great
dragon warden to absorb his power and rule the kingdom
herself. Transformed into a weredragon by the powerful ritual
that fused the warden’s power with her cold heart, Forlorne
now takes to the skies, feasting on all who challenge her and
cursing innocent villagers to become ravenous weredrakes.
The people called on the brave defenders of the realm, the
Knights of Whelvia, to protect them—but the knights instead
bent the knee to the draconic tyrant, allowing her to command
their forces and leaving the land without protectors.
In a Reign of the Weredragon campaign, you play destined
heroes of Whelvia, rising up against Forlorne Lykona and her
knights to save this once-idyllic land from the jaws of tyranny.
This campaign frame starts on page 128.

DARK HEART OF ANDALURIA
As the nights grow long in a land of rich wine and ancient
superstitions, a band of monster hunters battles the creatures
that stalk the shadows.
Designed by Carlos Cisco, Rue Dickey, Rowan Hall, and Rob Hebert
Complexity Rating: •••
The Pitch:
Andaluria is a land of sweeping vineyards where beauty and
dread intertwine. By day, the streets and valleys are alive
with festivals, music, and the scent of wine—but when the
sun sets, monsters come out to feast. For generations, the
old superstitions and folk rites kept the beasts at bay, but
the nights have grown unnaturally long, and the citizens of
Andaluria live in fear of increasingly terrifying monsters.
In a Dark Heart of Andaluria campaign, you’ll play monster
hunters who must investigate horrific crimes, navigate
political strife, and slay supernatural creatures to protect the
people from eternal darkness.
This campaign frame starts on page 144.
JOURNEY TO HORIZON
After a thousand-year cataclysm, a fellowship of heroes
embarks from their magically protected sanctuary to journey
across a broken continent and resurrect the fallen goddess who
can heal their world.
Designed by James Haeck, Rob Hebert, James Introcaso, and
Spenser Starke
Complexity Rating: ••••
The Pitch:
Long ago, the vast continent of Valloren was home to
wondrous landscapes shaped by the goddess Aurelia, wielder
of the elemental essence called terrana. But when her
disciples’ betrayal threatened to extinguish magic forever,
Aurelia sacrificed her own life to call down the stars and purge
the land of corruption. To protect her people from annihilation,
Aurelia raised magical barriers that would last a thousand
years.
In a Journey to Horizon campaign, you play heroes chosen
by fate to leave their recently unsealed sanctuary and travel
across a turbulent and hostile world on a quest to resurrect
the goddess.
This campaign frame starts on page 158.

Chapter 4: Castle High

TONE & FEEL
Adventurous, Dreamy, Full-Hearted, Melodramatic,
Modern, Playful, Thrilling
THEMES
Coming of Age, Curiosity & Rebellion, Friendship & Loyalty,
Magical vs. Modern
TOUCHSTONES
Kids on Brooms, Kiki’s Delivery Service, The Legend of Zelda:
Skyward Sword, Little Witch Academia, Onward, The Owl
House, She-Ra and the Princesses of Power, Slugblaster

OVERVIEW

Castle High

If your group decides to play this campaign, give your players the following information before character creation.

Modern civilization has come a long way. Industry. Innovation.
Plastic. The elders have seen horses give way to cars, science
catch up with magic, sending spells all but abandoned for
cell phones, and the gods replaced by pop stars. Much has
been lost, but more has been gained, and most people live
long, comfortable lives that involve little in the way of slaying
monsters or protecting kingdoms. The future is bright, and the
skies are mostly clear. Mostly.
But it wasn’t always this way. Long ago, in a time of great
danger, large portions of the earth were torn from the surface
and raised into the air by powerful crystals buried deep within
the land—crystals that became known as skyshards. No one
knows what caused the shards’ power to activate, but when
they did, they took castles, forests, and entire towns into
the clouds with them. Smaller skyshards could be attached
to mundane objects and vehicles, and these skybound
innovations allowed people to navigate the new world above.
The lands held aloft by skyshards became known as the
sky islands (usually shortened to skylands). Each island is
said to hold unique magical energy and host treacherous
secrets. Some contain ancient ruins, remnants of long-dead
civilizations visited by only the bravest adventurers and most
dedicated scholars. Those who study these ancient citadels
believe they were purposefully constructed around skyshards
to harness their power.
Today, people live in many of the villages, fortresses, and
homes that were raised into the sky so many centuries ago,
their buildings and technologies evolving with their needs.
Other skylands are only recently inhabited, with daring
entrepreneurs building malls for magical goods, hotels for
weary adventurers, and diners that drift through the clouds.
Smaller skylands are claimed by recluses who construct small
homesteads on portions of rock they can pilot through the
skies. Still more are entirely uninhabited—inhospitable, filled
with wild magic, and teeming with beasts too powerful to
tame.
One sky island holds a massive castle. This ancient edifice is
a prestigious high school where young people from all over
enroll to study magic, train with swords, soar through the
skies, and sit through algebra. Everyone calls it Castle High.
Sought after for its premier education and location, Castle
High invites students from across the realm to learn from
expert teachers. Here, the next generation of adventurers,
magicians, fighters, and sky explorers train among the clouds.
Castle High is a boarding school—new students are grouped
into small teams and assigned a shared dormitory within one
of four unique towers. Though each student takes their own
classes, Castle High also doles out “tower grades” based on
a team’s ability to collaborate on extracurricular projects.
Defined by the teaching style and preferences of their tower
dean, each group at Castle High receives a unique education
tailored to their “individual goals and styles of learning.” Or, at
least, that’s what it says in the brochure.

In their tower dorms, students study together, live together,
and fight over sink space. In their classes, they pass notes in
homeroom, doodle hexes on their binders, and get sent to
detention. And between it all, they sneak out to explore and
to find answers to the sky’s biggest questions—maybe now
more desperately than ever.
Over the past school year, eight kids have gone missing
exploring the skylands—far more than have ever been lost
before. It’s all the older students could talk about during
orientation. The school has stayed silent on the matter, and no
teacher will say anything about the disappearances, much less
mention the kids by name.
Even so, the students have heard (and spread) rumors
of something sinister happening out among the clouds,
something they think the grown-ups might be trying to hide.
Some kids are whispering that all the missing students
were members of one tower, and their tower dean caused
their disappearance. Others claim they were cult initiates or
were snapped up by a ravenous dragon. Some—especially
the younger kids—are saying that the mysterious “Night
Snatcher” who roams the towers got them. One particularly
prevalent rumor claims that the missing kids discovered
something in the school, and Headmaster Fellowes (she/her)
got rid of them to keep it a secret.
Adding fuel to this rumor, Headmaster Fellowes (who led
the school for four decades) didn’t come back this semester.
Instead, newly installed Headmaster Dove (they/them) took
over. Formerly the head of the Arcana Department, they were
known for their boisterous energy and creative approach to
teaching. But now, Dove’s demeanor is different—they’re
more serious and much stricter about the rules. Dove won’t
talk about Fellowes’s apparent departure, and they sent a kid
to detention during orientation for using an illusion spell to
hang a banner commemorating their missing friend.
With a new headmaster and all the celebration that comes
with orientation, most people were hoping to put the
tragedies in the past. But on the fifth night of orientation
week, right after the big dance, a student named Riley Averill
disappeared. Some kids have said Riley was acting strangely
the day before their disappearance, but nobody has come
forward with any more information. Their broom is missing,
but they left their backpack and private journal behind in their
tower room.
No one knows what to do. Students are panicking, and the
adults are pretending nothing is wrong. The school year is off
to an unnerving start, and one thing is for sure: something
strange is going on at Castle High.

Castle High
COMMUNITIES

All communities are available in a Castle High campaign. As needed, provide the following information to your players and
choose one or more of the questions to ask them during your session zero.

All Communities
Castle High is a campus where students of all backgrounds
study and live together miles away from their homes. And
while the towers, majors, cliques, and hierarchies of Castle
High might quickly feel more important than their upbringing,
each student arrives with a history and culture that help shape
their life in the castle.
ANCESTRIES

•	 How does your community feel about Castle High? Did
they help you go, make you go, or try to stop you?
•	 Who from your community do you miss most? What
unique way have they promised to communicate with you
while you’re away?
•	 What about living here feels very different from home?
What feels familiar?

All ancestries are available, but some have unique aspects in a Castle High campaign. As needed, provide the following
information to your players.

All Ancestries
This modern fantasy world includes all ancestries. You’ll find
elves wearing jeans, fungril watching TV, and ribbets shopping
in grocery stores.
Regardless of their lifespan, all ancestries in a Castle High
campaign go through a period of adolescence.
CLASSES

Faeries & Aetheris
Naturally winged, faerie and aetheris students zip around the
campus with ease. A player choosing an ancestry with flight
should consider how this informs their choice of skyshard
artifact (see “The Skyshards” on page 125). They can still
choose a skyshard if they’d like to have one for aesthetic
reasons, but their flight isn’t dependent on it.

All classes are available, but some have unique aspects in a Castle High campaign. As needed, provide the following information
to your players.

Beastbound Rangers
At Castle High, many Beastbound ranger students bond with
an animal companion that can fly. If a player wants to use their
animal companion as a flying mount, consider what happens
if their companion is forced out of the scene and that PC no
longer has a means to fly.
A ranger can incorporate their skyshard into their companion’s
saddle or use it as a trinket that allows them to communicate
with and call their mount. During character creation, discuss
how the ranger and their companion navigate the skies
together.
Druids
The Beastform options available to a Tier 1 druid don’t include
one with flight, so players who want to rely on their Beastform
for flight won’t have access right away. A druid character can
rely on their skyshard artifact until Tier 2, or the player can
work with the GM to modify a Tier 1 Beastform option to have
wings.

Chapter 4: Castle High

Syndicate Rogue
Though the Syndicate rogue’s “Contacts Everywhere” feature
can certainly be used when visiting other skylands outside
Castle High, players might also consider using this feature
around campus, such as when visiting a rival tower or when
another school comes to visit for a sports or academic
competition.
Winged Sentinel Seraphs
The “Wings of Light” class feature grants flight. As Winged
Sentinel seraphs already have a means to fly, players should
consider how this informs their choice of skyshard artifact
(see “The Skyshards” on page 125). They can still choose a
skyshard if they’d like to have one for aesthetic reasons, but
their flight isn’t dependent on it.

PLAYER PRINCIPLES

Castle High

If your group decides to play this campaign, give your players the following information before character creation.

Cast Spells, Wear Sneakers
Play a modern teenager in a fantastical world, reinterpreting
character details in a contemporary context. Does your
character keep their spells in a three-ring binder? Do they
decorate their shield with stickers? What’s the name of that
katari rock band they’re obsessed with?
Do Your Homework
One day, your character will be a hero, but today they’re a
student. Whether they’re a teacher’s pet, a rebel, or a would-
be legend who just wants to save the world already, they have
to deal with school. So take time to explore that side of the
game. Who’s their favorite teacher? How are their grades?
Yes, the world is in peril, and yes, their boyfriend just dumped
them, but right now, the real problem is that their chemistry
paper is due in four hours, and they haven’t even started.
Play in the Clouds
Students explore the skylands for many reasons, such as
treasure, knowledge, or investigating their fellow students’
disappearances. But it’s also fun! Young people have a strong
appetite for adventure, and Castle High campaigns are great
for excited, proactive PCs who do things for the joy of it.
Describe them flying, doing tricks, feeling the sunshine on
their skin. Horse around. Hang out a bit. Poke things with
sticks. Have them laugh after a dragon nearly eats them, then
show off their gnarly bruises. Go make some memories.

Fly for Your Life
Castle High can have its fair share of battles, but teenage
adventure stories often feature other kinds of action—
especially chases. Your character won’t be able to fight every
monster head-on. They’ll need to keep out of biting range, lead
adversaries into traps, and make them eat dust. The sky is
their battlefield, and flight is their most powerful weapon. So
when they see that big monster, take off!
Feel like a Kid
No matter how fantastical your character is, they’re also just
a normal kid going through the same things kids have gone
through forever: growth, change, heartbreak, caring too much
about a pair of jeans, and pretending to be adults until the
moment they suddenly are. Your character might have grown
from a spore or be able to breathe fire, but when you describe
their feelings, they become grounded and relatable.
Search out Answers
With the adults working hard to keep the missing students
hush-hush, ensure your character has a strong motivation to
search for answers. Maybe one of the missing kids was their
neighbor growing up, they developed a connection to Riley
during orientation, or their best friend is obsessed with finding
the missing students and your character’s doing their best to
support them. Whatever works best for your character, tie
them into the mystery in a meaningful way.
119
Chapter 4: Castle High

Castle High
GM PRINCIPLES
Keep the following guidance in mind while you GM this campaign.
Synthesize the Modern and the Fantastical
Everyone at the table will modernize elements of Daggerheart
throughout play, but they’ll look to you to set the tone and
guardrails. Are you going for something general (“early 21st
century, phones, jeans, and sneakers”) or specific (“2003,
social media, Y2K fashion”)? Modernize certain things and
leave others alone—maybe flashlights have replaced torches,
but the students use swords because modern weapons don’t
work on magical beasts.
Cut to the Chase
The setting and tools in Castle High are designed to support
thrilling aerial escapes, but it’s up to you to tee things up.
Create enemies who can fly, and challenge the PCs with foes
too powerful to face head-on. And when it’s time for a chase,
don’t wait for them to run. Just say this magic phrase: “It
starts chasing you! Where are you heading?”
Keep It Emotionally Grounded
No matter how strange the world or how high the fantasy, if
the people feel real, the story will, too. Let your NPCs behave
realistically, feel normal emotions, and care about the things
teenagers (or teachers) actually would. Emotional truth can
ground even the most fantastical scenes.
120
Chapter 4: Castle High

Run a School in the Sky
Castle High is a living place—it exists to push and pull on
the characters with rigid structure, dynamic characters, and
high expectations. The teachers have relationships and goals.
The students form factions and follow trends. The school has
rules, and those rules are enforced. Every time the students
meet a new NPC, write down their name, motive, and one
small detail about how they look or talk. Within a few sessions,
you’ll have a bustling campus.
Build an Aerial Playground
Design skylands that are fun for teenagers to explore.
Describe architecture that’s fun to fly through, such as
narrow gaps, ramps, or chunks of winding staircase. Place
strange objects behind mysterious doors. Create levers for
them to pull, figuratively and literally. Entice them with areas
that are safe to mess around in and areas so dangerous
they’re a puzzle just to navigate. Give them problems they
can’t immediately solve and toys they can’t immediately see
the purpose of, then look to the players to concoct clever
solutions.

DISTINCTIONS
Use this information to prepare your campaign. You can also share it with your players as needed.
The School
Castle High has been around as long as anyone remembers.
Students constantly debate its age, its history, the original
purpose of each chamber, and whether Dean Lesher (he/him)
was hired by the principal or simply freed from his coffin when
the east wing of the castle was being renovated.
The castle is built of hewn granite on a mass of jagged
bedrock, with a particularly large skyshard jutting out of
its base. The island can be piloted to specific destinations,
but it typically follows the trade winds in a yearlong circuit,
anchoring at occasional port towns along the way to resupply.
Experts in their field aim to teach at Castle High because it
funds and facilitates its faculty’s research. Many teachers
have their own goals beyond classroom instruction. Some
view teaching as a chore or an opportunity to push their
projects forward, while others consider it a duty. A few even
enjoy teaching for its own sake.
DOMAINS AS FIELDS OF STUDY
In Castle High, domains represent areas of study. Students
are free to take any courses they want, but they must focus
most of their studies on the two domains that make up their
class. Around campus, a student studying to become a wizard
might share their Codex course notes with a classmate looking
to become a bard while a druid student scurries by them, late
to a botany class for their studies in Sage. Meanwhile, a Blade
domain fencing course might be intended for students hoping
to become warriors and guardians, but that doesn’t stop
students with a variety of academic interests from enrolling.
THE CAMPUS
The campus is full of locations where students study,
socialize, and relax between it all.
Armory: This bustling place holds crowded workbenches,
weapon racks, and bins of miscellaneous survival gear. It’s a
common meeting place for Blade courses. They keep the good
stuff locked in a sentient chest. Only a few teachers have a key.
Atrium: This campus garden has seen better days, but it still
hosts an impressive variety of flora. It’s a common meeting
place for Sage courses. The atrium is always accepting
donations of wild flora, and the teachers won’t ask where
students got them.
Catacombs: The catacombs are the deepest part of the
school, accessible only by winding spiral staircases. Many
Dread courses are located in these caverns. Strange,
otherworldly sounds echo through the halls of the catacombs,
but nobody seems to be able to locate their source.
Clerestory: In this sunlit chamber, students pray, carve
their initials into pews, and take Splendor courses.
The intricate stained glass contains three words in an
unknown language.

Castle High
Courtyard: The Castle High quad is the school’s social hub,
where students eat lunch, gossip in study groups, and practice
broom tricks. A statue of the school’s mysterious founder was
vandalized last week with the word “liar.”
Forgotten Corridors: A place of shadows, the corridors
are where kids go to play truth or dare, hold clandestine
meetings, and take secret Midnight courses not on the official
curriculum. Older students have a map they pass around, but it
has never been finished.
Gymnasium: With weights, sparring rings, and storied locker
rooms, the gym is the common meeting place for Bone
courses, assemblies, and the occasional school dance. Every
morning, the floor is covered in ashes, and no one knows why.
Landing: This large open-air platform is used for unloading
skyships, stabling mounts, learning to fly, and playing broom
sports. A pair of cranky old manticores sleep behind the stables.
Library: This archive houses books, maps, and a computer
room possibly older than the castle itself—and at least
one ghost. Codex courses are commonly held within its
collections. They say the ghost will tell you a secret if you tell
her one first.
Ramparts: Castle High’s main observation platform is also the
common meeting place for Valor courses. A mounted telescope
is used to monitor the nearby skylands, but it can also be used to
spy on campus.
Theater: Here you’ll find musical instruments, costumes, and
a couple of students making out in the tech booth. The theater
is a common meeting place for Grace courses and school
assemblies. Sometimes the stage lights flash in a mysterious
pattern no one can decipher or control.
Vents: The system that steers Castle High uses massive
exhaust vents on the bottom of the skyland. The mists here
are heavy with magic and make it a common meeting place
for Arcana courses. I bet you can’t make it through the tunnels
before they turn the air vents on!

Chapter 4: Castle High

Castle High
CASTLE HIGH TOWERS
Students at Castle High are first sorted into four towers.
Within each tower, they’re split into teams of 2–5 students
known as tower groups. Students in a tower group share
a dorm room, work on group projects together, and are
expected to help each other. Each group is given a tower
grade based on their class scores, participation in projects and
extracurriculars, and general behavior.
While the characters typically have no choice where they go,
the players should select their tower together, because their
choice will influence the style of the campaign they’re playing.
The remaining towers can be brought into the story as the
homes of friendly classmates, bitter rivals, or crushes living
across campus.
Zenith
The tallest tower in the castle is overseen by Dean Parsons
(she/her), a peppy eccentric with pencils in her hair and
no time for paperwork. She loves teaching but dislikes the
classroom, preferring to give students assignments that get
them out of the school and in over their heads.
Choose Zenith if you want a mission-based campaign where
school assignments often require you to explore other
skylands.
Are these strange missions part of some greater purpose?
What does Parsons mean when she says you’ve “been chosen
for a reason”?
If players choose Zenith tower, consider how someone or
something on the surrounding skylands plays a prominent
part in the mystery of the missing kids.
Star
Castle High’s starboard tower (or simply Star) is overseen
by Dean “Coach” Hallister (he/him), a gruff gym teacher
who’s nearly as intense as his aftershave. Coach structures
each school year as a multi-event tournament complete with
jerseys, prizes, and every team’s grades on a giant scoreboard.
Choose Star if you want a structured campaign about
competitive underdogs, tower rivalries, and learning to work
as a team.
Why is Coach so hard on you? Does he see your potential or
think you’re losers—or is this tournament rigged?
If players choose Star tower, consider how a competition
or tournament at the school plays a prominent part in the
mystery of the missing kids.

Bower
Bow Tower (called Bower by students) is nominally overseen
by Dean Lin (they/them), a famously easygoing, chronically
absent teacher usually sleeping one off. Most students use
this freedom to slack off and party, but some use it as an
opportunity to pursue their own adventuring goals unimpeded.
Choose Bower if you want a more player-driven campaign
about independent young adventurers and opportunists.
Is Lin really as uninterested as they seem? Why are they tired
all the time? Are their headaches a cover for something else?
If players choose Bow tower, consider how the failings
of the adults in Castle High play a prominent part in the
mystery of the missing kids.
Stern
Stern Tower is overseen by Dean Lesher (he/him), a strict
teacher with an old-fashioned teaching style and zero
tolerance for nonsense. The windows are barred, and curfew
is early. Delinquents go in and honors students come out,
rebuilt by drills, discipline, and rote memorization. Of course,
some students just refuse to be taught.
Choose Stern if you want a more player-driven campaign
about rebellious students sneaking out, getting into trouble,
and learning things they shouldn’t.
What’s Lesher hiding? A scheme to take over the school?
A shrine to the Demon Lord? A sensitive side and good
intentions?
If players choose Stern tower, consider how the themes
of freedom and control play a prominent part in the
mystery of the missing kids.
Lock
The portside tower is sealed off. Everyone calls it Lock Tower,
and students whisper about what’s inside, how to get in, and
why a single window lights up every midnight.
GMs can use Lock Tower as an adventure hook or a space for
the table to create their own tower.
Transferring Towers
Your table might want to try a few towers during the
campaign. In this case, you could say that groups transfer
to new towers each time Castle High completes its circuit,
representing a single grade of high school.
Additionally, a midyear transfer might be required in the event
of expulsion, faculty restructuring, or some other school
scandal.

The Missing Kids
Something has been causing students to go missing. During
your session zero, ask the players for rumors about what
caused their disappearance and gather ideas from their
character building and map creation to come up with the
answer. Alternatively, you can choose an option from the list
below. Then select a few additional rumors to create multiple
potential threats, ensuring there are many avenues for players
to explore before uncovering the answer.
•	 An ancient creature of dark magic has been unleashed
on a nearby skyland.
•	 A teacher is trying to summon a powerful deity or
monster from another realm of existence to harness
their power, and they’ve been using students as bait.
•	 A band of sky pirates has been recruiting young
members as crew.
•	 A huge dragonshark has been hunting in the clouds
surrounding the school.
•	 A magical storm is teleporting kids to skylands on the
other side of the world.
•	 A powerful and corrupt sorcerer is using the hidden
basement within the deepest chambers of the school
as a workshop for their nefarious experimentation on
students.
RILEY AVERILL
There are nine missing students—including one who’s
particularly close to the PCs named Riley Averill. Riley was
a member of the PC’s tower group, and they bonded with
everyone over the first five days of orientation. They were
ready to spend the next year hanging out, studying, and living

The PCs should all have a connection to and care about Riley,

Riley’s Journal
Riley left their journal behind when they disappeared, and you
can use it to drop clues to your players about the mystery.
Before your first session, handwrite a journal entry on a piece
of lined paper from Riley’s point of view about orientation
week. Make sure to include references to specific moments of
orientation the players created during your session zero. Then,
near the end, include some ominous message like:
“I still don’t know who to trust with what I know about the
disappearances. For now, it all has to stay a secret until I can
find out more.”
Lastly, decide where you want to send the players to gather
clues about the students’ disappearances and add a final
sentence to the journal entry that hints at that location. For
example, if you want to send them to the stables, the journal
might say, “I’m headed to go feed Willis. That calms me
down.” Record the name “Willis” to drop later as one of the
griffins who lives in the stables.
When players investigate Riley’s journal, describe it as having
every page ripped out except for one near the back of the
book, then give them your written page to read. Between
every session (or so), prepare a new journal page for them to
discover. Throughout the entries, include clues, red herrings,
relationship drama, Riley’s thoughts about the PCs, and
anything else that gives further insight into Riley and the
mystery that led to their disappearance.
